subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Find the equation of the ellipse whose focus is (1, 2), eccentricity is 2/3 and directrix is 2x + 3y + 6 = 0.

steps.label: Set up SP = e·PM
steps.margin_note: First mark. By the focus-directrix property, the ellipse is the locus of points P with SP = e·PM.
steps.memory_tip: SP over PM equals e — write this ratio first, before touching any coordinates.
lines: By the focus-directrix property, SP/PM = e
steps.why: The locus of a point whose distance from a fixed point (the focus), divided by its distance from a fixed line (the directrix), is a constant e < 1, is by definition an ellipse.
common_mistakes: Computing √(4+9) as something other than √13 in the denominator.
Mixing up which point is the focus and which line is the directrix.

steps.label: Square and substitute coordinates
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Squaring both sides removes the root and the modulus together.
steps.memory_tip: e² = 4/9, and 13 in the denominator comes from squaring √13.
steps.why: Squaring both sides of the equation clears the square root on the left and the modulus on the right; the 117 comes from multiplying (2/3)² = 4/9 by 13, then clearing that fraction.
common_mistakes: Losing track of the 13 when clearing denominators, and multiplying by 9 alone instead of 117.

steps.label: Expand both sides
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Expand (2x+3y+6)² fully — it has three cross terms, not one.
steps.memory_tip: A trinomial squared has THREE cross terms: 2·(first·second), 2·(first·third), 2·(second·third).
steps.why: (2x + 3y + 6)² expands with three cross terms — 12xy, 24x and 36y — because it is a sum of three parts, not two; missing any one of them changes the final equation.
common_mistakes: Expanding (2x+3y+6)² as if it only had two terms, dropping one of the three cross terms.
Forgetting to multiply the whole right-hand side by the outer factor of 4.

steps.label: Simplify to the final equation
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. This is an oblique ellipse — its axes are not parallel to the coordinate axes.
steps.memory_tip: A nonzero xy term in the final equation always signals an oblique (tilted) conic.
lines: This equation represents an oblique ellipse —
its axes are not parallel to the x- and y-axes.
steps.why: Collecting all terms on one side gives the final second-degree equation; the surviving xy term (−48xy) is the algebraic signature that this ellipse's axes are tilted, not aligned with the coordinate axes.
common_mistakes: Trying to force the answer into x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 form, which is only possible for an axis-aligned ellipse.
Making an arithmetic slip while collecting the x² or y² coefficients across the two sides.
